criterion_notes.c1: Examines water supply and wastewater/sewerage service provision in Finland across urban population centres (municipal and supramunicipal utilities) and rural areas (water cooperatives, private wells/boreholes, and unconnected rural properties).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — broadly describes institutional, legal, and governance arrangements in Finland, including municipal self-government, taxation/subsidies, the Water Services Act of 2001, outsourcing, and cooperative organization. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — although it mentions statutory municipal responsibility, full cost-recovery charges/wastewater fees, and cooperative vs. municipal ownership, these are presented only as descriptive macro-governance and historical sector background rather than examined as rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access or exclusion. Because the paper also fails c3 (non-empirical narrative overview) and c5, the overall full-text decision is exclude under both readings.
criterion_notes.c3: NO — this is a narrative historical and institutional country overview synthesizing secondary statistics and prior reports (e.g., Dexia, Finnish Environment Institute, and prior dissertations/projects cited in Footnote 1), with no empirical research methods, no primary data collection or analysis, and no systematic review methodology (exclude as E05).
criterion_notes.c4: Cites secondary national historical figures in passing (e.g., population served by public water utilities increasing from 2.6 million to 4.6 million and per-capita water consumption declining after the 1974 wastewater fee and energy crisis), but does not measure or evaluate an empirical access outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: NO — lacks an identifiable empirical study design, sample, and defined exposure-outcome analysis.

evidence_quotes.quote: The paper aims at analysing and describing the Finnish experience from water and sanitation services, and especially the role of local governments in that context.

The paper first describes the role of local governments in the Nordic and European context and then deals with the diversity of the provision and production of water and sanitation services in Finland.
The Water Services Act of 2001 states specifically that the responsibility for water services and their development lies with the municipalities.
Firstly, during that period, the number of people served by public water utilities increased from 2.6 million to 4.6 million.
Municipally run water distribution and sewerage networks were built only in population centres, while those living in rural areas had to come up with their own water supply and sewerage systems.

raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Full text (15 pages) matches the record metadata and presents a narrative historical and institutional overview of municipal administration, public-private cooperation, and rural water cooperatives in Finland's water and wastewater sector. It reports no empirical research design, data collection methods, primary empirical analysis, or systematic synthesis methodology, and treats legal/governance structures only as descriptive macro-institutional background rather than empirically analyzing a rule-type mechanism governing service access.
